messages.subject: Occu Goodness of fit & Chat value issues
parts:
I'm hoping someone can provide some insight into my goodness of fit results. 
I'm using Occu() function and I'm interested in detection probabilities of 11 species from my very large camera trap survey. I have ~40 sampling occasions (7 days per occasion) and ~1000 sites.

When testing goodness of fit with mb.gof.test with nsim=1000, some species have chat values that look okay, but other species have chat values in the thousands, and two species that output chat=Inf.....maybe that just means my models dont adequately fit the data, but it seems rather outrageous to get chat values in the thousands or infinite chat, which leads me to believe I'm making some sort of error somewhere? 

The strangest part to me is that the largest chat values correspond to the species with the most detections...
If anyone can provide some insight, I would be extremely appreciative!

Best regards,
Carly

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Occu Goodness of fit & Chat value issues
parts:
Dear Carly,

to this, "The strangest part to me is that the largest chat values correspond to the species with the most detections...", a cynic might simply comment that GoF tests are often merely a test of whether your sample size is big enough to detect the violation of your model's assumptions.

But more seriously, yes, basically, a high value of the test statistic says that your data are extraordinary under the parametric assumptions of your model. And I would think that a result of infinity means that somewhere along the calculations to arrive at that test statistic there was a division by zero. Or perhaps some value that became too small or too large for R.

One thing that came to my mind is that 40 occasions is huge. I would never fit an occupancy model to such data, although this is of course not wrong. But I think that you can gain a lot by lumping your data, say, into 4 occasions of 10 days each. This will make detection probability higher (which is always a good thing with capture-recapture methods) and moreover, it will tend to reduce temporal autocorrelation in your response. This latter may be one of the mechanisms that contribute to the lack of fit of your data: when animals move around in some area, perhaps they hang our in the area of one trap for a couple days and then move on. This will result in a tendency of 1's to be followed by 1's at a given trap (and 0's by 0's), which is a violation of the usual assumption of independence. It could be addressed by modeling trap-dependence, but if you can make it go away, then that would be even better.

I am sure that this is at best a partial remedy to your problems, but I would explore this avenue a little.

Best regards --  Marc

Nevertheless, I would try to aggregate even further, but then also consider to model open populations. 40 weeks appears very long to make the closure assumption, and you might have to allow the presence/absence states around each trap to change over time.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Occu Goodness of fit & Chat value issues
parts:
Hi Carly,

I agree with Marc. It seems like you are likely dealing with seasonal variation in species-specific occupancy (hibernation/migration depending on the season) and should consider a dynamic model to explicitly account for those changes across the 9-month period. Perhaps, 3 3-month seasons would be more appropriate? The good news is that you should be able to use almost the exact same data format and code that you already have and just update to unmarkedMultiFrame and colext. Hope that helps!

Good luck!

Cheers,

Mike

messages.author: b5fd3d9c7b6c7b43
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Occu Goodness of fit & Chat value issues
parts:
Hi Carly,

Yes, I misunderstood the original framework (you do not need to run dynamic models if sites were not run in a repeated framework), but I would still recommend trying a dynamic model for the 6 months that the cameras were out, especially since I think you are capturing end of spring, summer, beginning of fall, which might exhibit differences in behavior, resources use, and movement of the species of interest. I think it's important to remember the assumptions of a single-season occupancy model (closure), especially in the context of a camera trap and the defined "site". I doubt that these sites are closed during the 6-month period, and much of the issues with detectability in camera trap surveys are confounded by that availability (e.g., temporary emigration), so I think you would have much more luck fitting models by accounting for those dynamics. Hope that helps!

Cheers,

Mike

Hi Mike & Marc,
Thanks a lot for your responses, I fixed my problem using your advice!

If I can ask one more question:
Since I'm not modeling the occupancy process (~detection covariates~1), do I still need to be concerned about spatial autocorrelation among my sampling sites? I know that I definitely have some level of spatial autocorrelation because my camera sites are only spaced a minimum of 1km from away from the next camera (ie. the assumption of independence between sampling sites is likely violated). If this is something I still need to be concerned with, is there a way to account for such spatial autocorrelation among sites?

Thanks in advance,

Carly
On Tuesday, August 13, 2019 at 8:38:29 AM UTC-4, Michael Cove wrote:

Hi Carly,

Yes, I misunderstood the original framework (you do not need to run dynamic models if sites were not run in a repeated framework), but I would still recommend trying a dynamic model for the 6 months that the cameras were out, especially since I think you are capturing end of spring, summer, beginning of fall, which might exhibit differences in behavior, resources use, and movement of the species of interest. I think it's important to remember the assumptions of a single-season occupancy model (closure), especially in the context of a camera trap and the defined "site". I doubt that these sites are closed during the 6-month period, and much of the issues with detectability in camera trap surveys are confounded by that availability (e.g., temporary emigration), so I think you would have much more luck fitting models by accounting for those dynamics. Hope that helps!

Cheers,

Mike

Should I still be using the dynamic model even though I have 2 years of data with different sites?
My sampling period is throughout the summer-- 500 sites May-October 2016 and 500 different sites May-October 2017. Since each site was only sampled for one season of one year, I thought it made sense to use the single season model! Let me know your thoughts, I appreciate the insight you have already provided!

I agree with Marc. It seems like you are likely dealing with seasonal variation in species-specific occupancy (hibernation/migration depending on the season) and should consider a dynamic model to explicitly account for those changes across the 9-month period. Perhaps, 3 3-month seasons would be more appropriate? The good news is that you should be able to use almost the exact same data format and code that you already have and just update to unmarkedMultiFrame and colext. Hope that helps!

Dear Carly,

to this, "The strangest part to me is that the largest chat values correspond to the species with the most detections...", a cynic might simply comment that GoF tests are often merely a test of whether your sample size is big enough to detect the violation of your model's assumptions.

But more seriously, yes, basically, a high value of the test statistic says that your data are extraordinary under the parametric assumptions of your model. And I would think that a result of infinity means that somewhere along the calculations to arrive at that test statistic there was a division by zero. Or perhaps some value that became too small or too large for R.

One thing that came to my mind is that 40 occasions is huge. I would never fit an occupancy model to such data, although this is of course not wrong. But I think that you can gain a lot by lumping your data, say, into 4 occasions of 10 days each. This will make detection probability higher (which is always a good thing with capture-recapture methods) and moreover, it will tend to reduce temporal autocorrelation in your response. This latter may be one of the mechanisms that contribute to the lack of fit of your data: when animals move around in some area, perhaps they hang our in the area of one trap for a couple days and then move on. This will result in a tendency of 1's to be followed by 1's at a given trap (and 0's by 0's), which is a violation of the usual assumption of independence. It could be addressed by modeling trap-dependence, but if you can make it go away, then that would be even better.

I am sure that this is at best a partial remedy to your problems, but I would explore this avenue a little.

Best regards --  Marc

I'm hoping someone can provide some insight into my goodness of fit results. 
I'm using Occu() function and I'm interested in detection probabilities of 11 species from my very large camera trap survey. I have ~40 sampling occasions (7 days per occasion) and ~1000 sites.

When testing goodness of fit with mb.gof.test with nsim=1000, some species have chat values that look okay, but other species have chat values in the thousands, and two species that output chat=Inf.....maybe that just means my models dont adequately fit the data, but it seems rather outrageous to get chat values in the thousands or infinite chat, which leads me to believe I'm making some sort of error somewhere? 

The strangest part to me is that the largest chat values correspond to the species with the most detections...
If anyone can provide some insight, I would be extremely appreciative!

Best regards,
Carly
